confidence_note: Full text not accessible; the serpent and Jaws passages are quoted consistently across several secondary sources. The old text's painter scene and quotes ('this voice comes from old injuries'; 'Ah, it's you, I recognise you') are not verified and are dropped. The 'monsters' list is a Week 1 exercise described by many readers; its exact wording is not quoted.
facts: Cameron calls the inner critic the Censor, a nasty internal and eternal critic.
She writes: 'Think of your Censor as a cartoon serpent, slithering around your creative Eden, hissing vile things to keep you off guard.'
If a serpent doesn't work for you, she suggests another cartoon image, perhaps the shark from Jaws; draw it, put an X through it, and post it where you write.
Making the Censor into the nasty, clever little character it is, she says, begins to pry loose some of its power.
She tells readers that the Censor's negative opinion is not the truth.
Morning pages help: by writing first thing every morning, you learn to evade the Censor, and because there is no wrong way to write them, its opinion doesn't count.
In the first week of the course, readers list historic 'monsters', people who damaged their creative self-worth, and 'champions' who encouraged it.
Cameron places the Censor in the logical (left) brain, and says that beyond the reach of its babble we find our own quiet center.
scene_details: a cartoon serpent slithering around a creative Eden
a drawing of the shark from Jaws with an X through it, pinned where you write
a list of old monsters and champions
tension: Cameron's answer to the voice that stops artists is to draw it as a cartoon and cross it out.
opening_idea: Start with the drawing: a cartoon serpent or the Jaws shark, an X through it, pinned above a desk.

lessons.idea: Give the critical voice a separate shape so you can hear it as one voice among others, not as the truth about your work.
lessons.anchor: Cameron's cartoon serpent and crossed-out shark turn the Censor into a character.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A cook who hears 'that'll be bland' before every new dish names that voice after a fussy relative and tastes the food anyway.

reflect_final: If your inner critic were a cartoon, what would it look like and what line would it hiss most often?

use_cases.situation: A friend says 'I'm not a real artist' about their hobby.
use_cases.move: Tell them Cameron's trick: draw that voice as a cartoon serpent, cross it out, and pin it above the desk.

use_cases.situation: Your child tears up a drawing because it's 'bad'.
use_cases.move: Ask what the 'bad' voice would look like as a cartoon and draw it together.

use_cases.situation: You hear 'this is stupid' before sharing an idea.
use_cases.move: Note the line on paper as the critic's, then share the idea anyway.

pocket_idea: Draw your inner critic as a cartoon and cross it out; a hissing snake is easier to ignore than the truth.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Julia Cameron tells blocked artists to draw their inner critic as a cartoon snake and put an X through it.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In The Artist's Way, Julia Cameron calls the inner critic the Censor. Her advice: picture it as a cartoon serpent hissing in your creative Eden, or the shark from Jaws. Draw it, cross it out, pin it where you work. Turning it into a nasty little character loosens its grip, and its opinion stops sounding like the truth.
